01

Definition & Bone Growth

Definition

is metabolic disorder due to failure of mineralization of osteoid tissue in growing bone.

  • It is unique to children and adolescents.
  • Failure of osteoid to calcify in adults is called Osteomalacia.

Factors needed for bone growth are:

  • Active epiphysial plate → cartilage formation → osteoid tissue → mineralization → bone
  • Process of mineralization needs active vitamin D, calcium, and phosphate.
Pathology: normally there are 2 types of ossification usually occur.

Subperiosteal → increase bone thickness.
Intra-cartilaginous → increase length of the bone.

Zones of epiphysisNormal end of long boneRacketic end of long bone
Resting cartilageSingle layer of osteoblastsSingle layer of osteoblasts
Zone of proliferating cartilage4-6 layers of cartilage cells (regular and avascular)Many layers of cartilage cells → irregular and vascular
Zone of degenerating cartilageSwollen cells and degenerated.
Matrix impregnated with Ca → appear as sharp line at end of the shaft		Failure of cartilage cells degeneration.
No Ca deposition → lower end of the shaft frayed and irregular.
Very vascular
↑ capillaries → provide osteoblasts → lay osteoid and secrete alkaline phosphatase.
Normal Ca/Ph ratio → mineralization of the osteoid occur.		Resorption of bone → replaced by uncalcified osteoid → rarefaction.
Fragile bone → fractures and deformities.
02

Classifications of Rickets

Essential Ca deficiency

Responsive to normal doses of vit D

  • Vitamin D deficiency rickets.

Responsive to large doses of vit D

  • Vitamin D malabsorption: Celiac disease, Crohn’s disease, Cystic fibrosis.
  • Chronic liver diseases.
  • Anticonvulsant drugsRenal glomerular disease
  • Hypocalcaemia vitamin D-dependent rickets type I

Essential phosphate deficiency

  • Inadequate intake of phosphate
  • Malabsorption or ingestion of Ph binders as antacids containing Al, Mg.
  • Renal tubular disorders (congenital or acquired)
  • Oncogenic rickets

End organ resistance to Vit D:

  • Hypocalcaemia vit D dependant rickets type II.

Condition resembling Rickets:

  • Hypophosphatasia
  • Metaphyseal dysostosis

Old classifications of rickets

Vitamin D def. rickets

Non-Vitamin D def. rickets

Refractory rickets

Concomitant rickets with

  • Chronic malabsorption
  • Chronic liver disease
  • Chronic glomerular disease
  • Antiepileptic drugs
  • Mesenchymal tumors

Inherited rickets

  • Vitamin D dependent rickets (AR)
  • Familial hypophosphatemia (XLD)
  • Fanconi syndromes:
    • Primary: sporadic or AR
    • Hereditary:
      • Cystinosis (Lignac S.) AR
      • Occulo-cerebro renal (Lowe S.) (XLR)
  • Rickets with renal tubular acidosis (Lightwood S.) AR

Conditions resembling rickets

  • Hypophosphatasia (AR)
  • Metaphyseal dysostosis
03

Vitamin D Deficiency Rickets

Causes of infantile rickets: decreased intake due to

  • Lack of rich sources of vitamin D as cod liver oil, fish, yoghurt, egg yolk, cheese
  • Giving rachitogenic diet
    • Poor in vitamin D as unfortified animal milk and carbohydrates or
    • Excess phytates or oxalates that prevent ca absorption as green leafy vegetables.

Lack of skin exposure to ultra violet rays:

  • Glass windows, clouds, and dust.
  • Excessive wrappings of the infants.
  • Dark coloured skin
NB. Breast milk have low vitamin D level but better than fresh cow milk due to:

Ca: Ph ratio is 2:1 which is optimum for bone mineralization.
Intestinal pH ideal for calcium absorption.
Lactalbumin compound with vitamin D → ↑ bioavailability.

Factors that can increase a child's risk of rickets include:

  • Sex: more in males (may be due to protective locus on X-chromosome)
  • Age: common between 6 months to 3 years & Race: common in black races.
  • Location: in cities than rural areas and in northern latitudes (less sun exposure),
  • Season: common in winter
  • Medications. especially anticonvulsants
  • Growth factors:
    • More common in growing child as premature and twins
    • Rare in arrested growth as PEM and cretinism → atrophic rickets
  • Maternal factors
    • Mother's vitamin D deficiency during pregnancy.
    • Exclusive breast-feeding (20-40 IU/L) while fortified powdered milk (400 IU/L).
04

Clinical Presentation & Early Rickets

Symptoms of rickets:

  • Delayed motor milestones
  • Delayed teething
  • Deformities in the long bones or skull
  • Bone pain ± fracture
  • Short stature
  • Constipation

Signs of rickets:

  • Early manifestations
  • Late or advanced manifestations
    • Skeletal
    • Non-skeletal

Early manifestation of rickets:

General manifestations:

  • anorexia, irritability, excessive sweating of forehead?

Craniotabes:

  • Skull bones yield under pressure like ping - pong or eggshell crackling sensations due to thinning of inner table of the skull.
  • Detected by pressing over occipital or parietal bone.
  • Disappear by the end of 1st year.

Racketic rosaries:

  • palpable enlargement of costochondral junctions (due to excess osteoid)
05

Late Rickets

1. Head

  • Large head with frontal & parietal bossing due to excess osteoid
  • Box shaped skull (caput quadratum)
  • Delayed closure of anterior fontanelle.
  • Depressed nasal bridge due to frontal bossing
  • Delayed teething and even caries.
  • Craniotabes (till the end of 1st year)

2. Chest manifestations

  • Rachetic rosaires: more visible and palpable, and non-tender.
  • Longitudinal sulcus lateral to the rosaries.
  • Harrison sulcus: transverse groove along the costal insertion of the diaphragm (due to pulling on the soft ribs).
  • Chest deformities:
    • Pigeon chest: sternum & adjacent cartilages project forwards.
    • Funnel chest: depression of the sternum & flaring out of the lower ribs.

3. Extremities

  • Broadening of epiphysis of long bones especially at wrist & ankles.
  • Marfan sign: transverse groove over the medial malleolus due to unequal growth of the two ossific centres.
  • Green stick fracture.
  • Deformities:
    • Bowing of the forearm in creeping child.
    • Bowlegs
    • Genu valgus (knock knee)
    • Genu varum
    • Genu recurvatum (over extended knee)

4. Pelvis:

  • Contracted inlet: due to forward projection of sacral promontory.
  • Contracted outlet: due to forward projection of coccygeal tip.
  • Both may lead to obstructed labour in later life.

5. Vertebral column:

  • Kyphosis:
    • In the dorso-lumbar region,
    • Smooth,
    • Apparent on sitting (disappear by lifting)
  • Compensatory lumber lordosis to the kyphosis.
  • Scoliosis: lateral curvature of the spine

Non skeletal manifestations: usually due to weakness of the muscles and ligaments

  • Delayed motor milestones.
  • Abdominal distension (pot belly abdomen): with or without umbilical hernia.
  • Ptosis of the liver & the spleen (also due to chest deformities).
  • Constipation: due to intestinal hypotonia.
  • Manifestations of complications as hypocalcaemia (tetany)
06

Complications & Differential Diagnosis

Skeletal complications

  • Permanent skeletal deformities: rare in vitamin D deficiency.
  • Disproportionate short stature (Rachitic dwarfism)
  • Obstructed labour later due to contracted pelvis

Non-skeletal complications

  • Respiratory infections & atelectasis due to limited chest expansion and hypotonia of respiratory muscles.
  • Gastroenteritis due to intestinal hypotonia → stasis → 2ry bacterial overgrowth.
  • Tetany: may occur in rickets with hypocalcaemia; rare in vit D deficiency
  • IDA is a common association.

Differential diagnosis of rickets

Delayed

  • Motor milestones or inability to walk.
  • Teething as
  • Closure of anterior fontanelle.

Craniotabes

  • As in Premature,
  • Hydrocephalus ( affect all bones
  • Osteogenesis imperfecta mainly frontal.
  • Congenital syphilis,
  • Hypervitaminosis A.

Causes of macrocephaly.

MACRO (Mucopolysaccharidosis, the same as before)

Scorbutic rosaries:

  • Due to defective collagen formation and subperiosteal hge.
  • Angular, tender, irregular with sternal depression.
  • Plus other clinical and radiologic features of scurvy

Pott’s disease (T.B of spine):-

  • Kyphosis is angular and persistent.
  • X-ray and CT spine is diagnostic,
DD from other causes of short stature:

(rickets cause disproportionate short stature with short limbs).
